title: Functions
summary: A function packages instructions so you can run them by name.

subtopics.title: Inputs
subtopics.explanation: A function is a named set of instructions that can receive inputs and return a result. Parameters name the inputs in its definition; arguments are the actual values supplied when calling it. For example, `formatDate(date)` receives one date. Clear inputs make a function reusable without relying on hidden global state. Choose a parameter shape that makes calls clear. A few simple inputs may be positional; a group of related options may be easier to pass as an object. Parameters are like labeled slots on a form; arguments are the values placed in those slots.

subtopics.title: Calling a function
subtopics.explanation: Calling a function runs its instructions. The argument is matched to its parameter by position unless the function uses an object argument. For example, `calculateTax(price)` passes the current price into the calculation. Choose names and parameter order that make a call understandable where it is used. When calling a function, pass values in the documented order and consider what happens when a value is missing. Defaults should represent an intentional fallback. Calling a function is like giving a recipe its ingredients and asking it to run.

subtopics.title: Returning a result
subtopics.explanation: `return` sends a result back to the caller and ends that path through the function. A formatting helper can return text for a label; a caller can store or display it. If a function uses braces but reaches the end without returning, its result is `undefined`. Return values make a function composable: another function can format, store, or display the result. Avoid mixing a returned result with unrelated side effects. A return value is like handing the finished item back to the person who requested it.

subtopics.title: Optional work
subtopics.explanation: Some functions perform an action and do not need to return a useful value. A click handler may open a menu or update state. That is still a function with a clear job. Use a returned result when another part of the program needs a value to continue its work. An action function may return nothing useful, but its name should state the action. Event handlers are easier to trace when their purpose is obvious. A function with no return can be like a doorbell: it triggers an action but gives no object back.

subtopics.title: One clear job
subtopics.explanation: Give each function one understandable responsibility and a name that describes it. `saveSettings` is clearer than `doThing`. Small functions are easier to test and reuse. If a function validates data, fetches it, formats it, and updates the page, separate those steps when that improves clarity. One responsibility makes tests focused. If a function needs many unrelated inputs or changes several different systems, consider separating its work. A focused function is like a single-purpose tool that is easy to find and use.

foundations.overview: A function is a reusable set of instructions that can receive values and return a result. It helps name a task and keep repeated logic in one place. Think of it like a small machine: inputs go in, work happens, and a result may come out. Call a function when you need its behavior, and give it one understandable responsibility.
foundations.whyItMatters: Functions organize logic behind names, inputs, and results. Small responsibilities support reuse, testing, and easier debugging.
foundations.browserPerspective: When a function is called, the engine pushes a new frame onto the call stack with its own execution context (its parameters, local variables, and `this`). When it returns, the frame is popped and control resumes at the caller.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Functions implement event handlers, validation logic, data transformations (map/filter/reduce callbacks), API request helpers, and the components and hooks of UI frameworks.
foundations.businessImpact: Well-factored functions make features faster to build and safer to change, directly affecting delivery speed and defect rates. Poorly scoped functions create tangled code that slows teams down.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Functions are the primary tool for abstraction and testing — small, single-purpose functions are easy to reason about, unit-test, and reuse across a codebase.
foundations.performanceImpact: Function calls are cheap and heavily optimized by modern engines, but creating many functions in hot loops (e.g., new closures per render) can add allocation pressure; hoist or memoize where it matters.
commonUseCases: Callbacks for events and array methods (map, filter, forEach)
Factory functions that build and return configured objects or functions
Variadic helpers that accept any number of arguments via rest params

commonMisconceptions.myth: JavaScript checks that you pass the right number of arguments.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It does not — missing parameters are `undefined` and extra arguments are silently ignored (but still in the arguments object).

commonMisconceptions.myth: Function expressions are hoisted just like declarations.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only the variable binding is hoisted; the function value is not assigned until that line runs, so calling it early throws.

visualExplorer.title: What happens when you call a function
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how the engine handles a function call from definition to returned value.

config.intro: Follow a call to add(2, 3) and see how parameters, the call stack, and return work together.

steps.name: Define the function
steps.detail: add(a, b) is created with parameters a and b and a body that returns a + b.

steps.name: Call add(2, 3)
steps.detail: The engine pushes a new frame onto the call stack with a = 2 and b = 3.

steps.name: Bind arguments to parameters
steps.detail: Arguments 2 and 3 are matched positionally to the parameters a and b.

steps.name: Execute the body
steps.detail: The expression a + b evaluates to 5 inside the function's own scope.

steps.name: Return the value
steps.detail: return 5 hands the result back to the caller and pops the frame off the stack.

steps.name: Use the result
steps.detail: The caller receives 5 and assignment or further expressions continue.

interactiveExamples.title: Declaration vs expression
interactiveExamples.explanation: A declaration can be called before it is defined; an expression cannot, because only the variable binding is hoisted.

interactiveExamples.title: Default and rest parameters together
interactiveExamples.explanation: Default parameters fill in missing values; rest parameters gather the remaining arguments into a real array.

codeLab.title: Write a variadic average()
codeLab.instructions: Implement average(...nums) that returns the arithmetic mean of any number of arguments using a rest parameter. Return 0 when called with no arguments.
hints: Use `...nums` to collect all arguments into an array.
Guard against an empty array before dividing to avoid NaN.

keyTakeaways: A function is a named set of instructions that can receive inputs and return a result.
Calling a function runs its instructions.
`return` sends a result back to the caller and ends that path through the function.
Some functions perform an action and do not need to return a useful value.
Give each function one understandable responsibility and a name that describes it.
